units.translation: But it is not, says Didymus (fr. I 5, 32 Schmidt 66), but a hymn to Demeter, like the oupingos among the Troezenians to Artemis. For oulos and ioulos is the sheaf gathered from the handfuls, and Ouliō is Demeter. Ioulos is also called a certain animal, a small many-footed creature; for it has many feet on each side, like the centipede. Theophrastus, in his letter to Phanias (fr. 185 Wimmer), says that it is also called onos, as in Sophocles in the Deaf Satyrs (fr. 363 Pearson): 'rolling like a donkey of equal weight'.
1 sch. Theocr. IV 50/51 c. d Et. Gen. (AB) ἁρμοῖ Hesych. Suid. ἁρμοῖ Eust. 140, 13 cf. Deicke 61, W 108

3 sch. II 43 Et. Gen. (AB) ἴουλος: the first sprouting of hair on the cheeks, from the ioulos animal, which has many and dense (καὶ π. om. B) feet, as Apollonius. For example II 40—43 (οἷον sqq. om. B). χνοάοντας instead of as down referring to the iouloi, and ἔτι instead of recently. It is also the name of a song, as Eratosthenes says in the Hermes: 'or a poor spinner walking on a high gate †δανδαί τις† sang beautiful iouloi' (ἡ χ. sqq. om. B). Tz. Lyc. 23, 17 Sch. Chil. 2 Et. Gen. (AB) Κλειτή: ... but Apollonius also adds a verse, for example I 976. I found a scholium on it, that she was the wife of Cyzicus and daughter of Merops of Percote (Περκῶτις A) by birth, a seer (in B everything from α τὴν μέν in the poet's words is missing). The accent is twofold, but the majority accent it acute. It means 'glorious', from κλειτός. Parthen. 28 Con. Narr. 41, 5 cf. Knaack Comm. phil. in hon. sod. phil. Gryph. 1887, 35
